candidate.educational_objective: Teach a client with chemotherapy-related neutropenia to use frequent hand hygiene and to report a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher or other infection symptoms immediately rather than delaying evaluation.

options.A: I will wash my hands often and call my oncology team right away if my temperature reaches 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, even if it happens at night.
options.B: If I develop a fever overnight, I can wait until the oncology office opens the next morning before reporting it.
options.C: Because my white blood cell count is already low, hand hygiene will not meaningfully affect my risk of infection.
options.D: I only need to report infection symptoms if they continue for several days or become severe enough to limit my activity.

candidate.rationale: Chemotherapy-related neutropenia increases infection risk. CDC guidance instructs patients receiving chemotherapy to wash their hands often, watch for signs and symptoms of infection, and call their clinician immediately for a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. CDC specifically states not to wait until morning if infection is suspected because infection during chemotherapy can be life-threatening. Delaying fever or infection reporting is therefore unsafe.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC states that chemotherapy-related neutropenia increases infection risk; patients should wash their hands often and call their clinician immediately for a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Suspected infection during chemotherapy is an emergency and should not be deferred until morning.
